webhook_hmac_verdict.evidence: REQ-181 (impl_order 354): 'secret (stored hashed -- see below, never returned once created)', with the AC 'stores only a hashed form in the database, and returns the plaintext exactly once as hmac_secret_once'. REQ-183 (impl_order 356): computes 'an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the JSON-encoded payload using the subscription's stored secret (REQ-181's schema)'. A cryptographic hash of the secret is not the secret; an HMAC keyed on the stored hash cannot be reproduced by a receiver holding the plaintext that was delivered once as hmac_secret_once. REQ-183's own AC compounds this: 'a test computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 signature from the same secret and payload and asserts it equals the value deliver/3 actually sent' -- that test is unsatisfiable as drafted, because signer and verifier cannot both hold the same key material. REQ-ANALYST's finding is correct and this batch surfaces rather than introduces the defect.
webhook_hmac_verdict.recommendation: BLOCK REQ-183 (letflow-queue task 356) FROM CLAIM UNTIL REQ-189 LANDS. REQ-189/190 are the right treatment of the underlying design question, but they are NOT sufficient protection on their own: REQ-183 is already registered and claimable NOW, and nothing in REQ-183's own text warns an implementer, who would build a signing path that cannot pass its own verification AC. REQ-183 does not need deletion or full redrafting -- its retry/backoff, auto-pause and DLQ-landing halves are sound and unaffected. Concretely: (1) ORCH holds/locks task 356 in letflow-queue so no agent claims it before REQ-189's decision record exists; (2) REQ-183 gains REQ-189 in its depends_on -- it currently has only [REQ-181, REQ-176] -- which is the durable fix, because the queue's own dependency gating then enforces the ordering without relying on anyone reading prose; (3) REQ-183's signing clause and its signature-verification AC are amended to resolve the key through REQ-189's chosen mechanism rather than 'the stored secret'. Because REQ-183 is an EXISTING pending entry, this is an edit rather than an append, so it falls outside this batch's append-only constraint and must be routed to REQ-ANALYST as a scoped amendment -- the same treatment REQ-179/180 got -- rather than left implicit.

req_189_183_edge_direction.reasoning: REQ-ANALYST removed REQ-183 from REQ-189's depends_on and kept REQ-189 in REQ-183's. That is the right direction on the semantics, not merely a convenient cycle-break. REQ-189's deliverable is a decision RECORD -- a document. Its input is REQ-183's already-written requirement TEXT, which exists in docs/requirements.yaml today and needs nothing built to be read. REQ-183's deliverable is code that cannot exist before the decision it implements. So the genuine 'must be finished first' relation runs REQ-189 -> REQ-183, and depends_on encodes build order, not reading order. Reversing it would have deadlocked the pair. The rationale is recorded inside REQ-189's own description ('reads REQ-181's and REQ-183's already-written TEXT as a drafting input, but does not need either to be BUILT first -- it is the decision that unblocks them, not the other way round'), which is the right place for a future reader. Widest set in the batch, but each edge traces to a specific AC. None superfluous, none missing.
req_201_validation.d_stage_fit: PASS -- S6; explicitly no route, correctly justified (R-Co has no alerts route and the SPA has no alerting client).
req_201_validation.e_size: PASS -- one subsystem, one mechanism, no route half needed. The 14 ACs map 1:1 onto detection, edge-triggering, delivery/retry and placement; no second deliverable smuggled in.
req_201_validation.central_claim_verified: CONFIRMED. src/obs/alerts.zig L6-11 declares AlertType with exactly four variants: instance_error_stuck, dlq_depth_threshold, scheduler_lag_threshold, webhook_subscription_paused -- and all four map to producers inside this stage, so the 'no external blocker' claim holds. RetryPolicy defaults (max_attempts 3, base_backoff_ms 1000, max_backoff_ms 30000, multiplier 2.0), AlertHookConfig fields (hook_id, enabled, destination_url, timeout_ms, auth_secret_ref, retry_policy) and AlertThresholds (error_stuck_minutes, dlq_depth_threshold, scheduler_lag_ms) all match the requirement's text field for field. File is 972 lines as stated.
req_201_validation.webhook_reuse_check: CORRECTLY HANDLED -- and better than mere reuse. REQ-201 does NOT duplicate REQ-183's dispatch path, but it also does not naively merge into it. It draws an explicit distinction the batch needed: alerting hooks are PLATFORM-OPERATOR diagnostics with four fixed triggers and NO DLQ landing, whereas webhook subscriptions are TENANT-FACING, tenant-configured, HMAC-signed, auto-pausing and DLQ-landing. An AC requires the moduledoc to state this 'so the two are not later merged'. Crucially it specifies the one behavioural difference that matters -- an exhausted alert delivery is LOGGED and does NOT create a dlq_entries row -- and asserts BOTH the log and the absence of the DLQ row. That is the correct call: these are genuinely different mechanisms that merely look alike, and collapsing them would have been the real defect.

issues.requirement: docs/migration/stage-6-operational-cross-cutting.md (Scope section) -- no requirement text is wrong
issues.title: The new exhaustiveness assertion is false: four src/repository files have no owning requirement
issues.detail: The doc now states 'This list is exhaustive: every other file in the subsystems above has a named owning requirement in the per-subsystem list'. Tested against R-Co's actual trees for all six subsystems. Five of six hold: src/scheduler (6: scheduler/store/recurrence/artifact_retention -> REQ-185-188, partition_maintenance/partition_retention -> named deferral), src/obs (5, now all named), src/expr (7: ast/lexer/parser/evaluator/error/mod -> REQ-197/198, benchmark -> named deferral), src/ordering (5 -> REQ-199), src/secrets (6 + integration/webhook_keys.zig -> REQ-189/190). src/repository DOES NOT. The doc claims 'src/repository (7 files) -- REQ-191-192', but REQ-191/192 cover only service_catalog.zig (REPO-07/SVC-01/03/04), and process_module_catalog.zig is a named deferral. That leaves FOUR files with no owning requirement and no deferral entry: activation.zig (192 lines, REPO-08/09/10, atomic multi-artifact activation), artifacts.zig (297 lines, REPO-01/02/03, content-addressed versioned artifact store), canonicaliser.zig (270 lines, REPO-01/04, canonical JSON + SHA-256 hashing) and schemas.zig (124 lines, REPO-05, form-schema indexing). mod.zig is a module aggregator and needs no separate owner. Confirmed unowned by search: the ONLY mention of artifact_versions anywhere in docs/requirements.yaml is REQ-109 declaring form_schema_registry/REPO-05 explicitly OUT OF SCOPE ('named explicitly because grepping "form schema" lands here first and would build the wrong mechanism'), and no requirement in the file is titled for an artifact store or repository port. This is exactly the defect the original MAJOR finding described, one subsystem over. FIX (three options, REQ-ANALYST's call): (i) draft requirements for the artifact store as REQ-202+, (ii) record all four as explicit deferrals with named blockers in the not-covered list -- most likely correct if no Letflow stage consumes a content-addressed artifact store yet, the same reasoning already applied to process_module_catalog.zig -- or (iii) if an earlier stage genuinely owns them, cite that stage in the per-subsystem list. What is NOT acceptable is leaving the exhaustiveness sentence standing while four files are unaccounted for.

non_blocking_observations: The exhaustiveness assertion, though currently false, is a genuine improvement in kind: a falsifiable claim that can be tested and was, versus the previous range that quietly implied coverage. Once ISSUE-4 is closed the doc becomes a real coverage contract for the stage.

REQ-200's decision to leave 'renaming versus emitting both fields' to the implementer is acceptable scoping, not vagueness -- the binding constraint (TimelineFeedItem.tsx must render unchanged) is stated as an assertable AC, so either implementation is verifiable.

REQ-201's placement handling is the strongest of the batch's three 0003-interaction cases: it actively argues AGAINST inheriting R-Co's global placement on Letflow-specific grounds rather than merely flagging the divergence.
REQ-183's amendment is confined to the signing clause, one AC and provenance text; the retry/backoff, auto-pause and DLQ-landing halves are untouched, as recommended.
All prior-iteration findings remain resolved; no regression introduced in REQ-185..REQ-199, whose depends_on sets are unchanged except REQ-190's fix.
rework_iteration_1.next_action: Rework REQ-ANALYST -- ONE targeted fix. Account for src/repository/activation.zig, artifacts.zig, canonicaliser.zig and schemas.zig: either draft them as REQ-202+, or add them to the stage doc's not-covered list with named blockers (likely correct, mirroring process_module_catalog.zig's treatment), or cite the earlier stage that owns them. The exhaustiveness sentence must be true or must be qualified. Everything else in the batch is validated and ready -- REQ-185..REQ-201 pass all five checks, and the REQ-183 amendment plus the REQ-189/183 edge direction are both endorsed. This is a doc-scope fix, not a requirement-text defect, so it should be a fast iteration.

rework_iteration_2.summary: PASS. The rework-1 MAJOR finding is fixed correctly and at the root: src/repository's four unowned files are now accounted for -- three drafted as REQ-202/203, one deferred with a real blocker -- and the exhaustiveness assertion is now TRUE, which I verified independently rather than accepting. REQ-202 and REQ-203, validated here for the first time, both PASS all five checks; every R-Co and in-tree claim they rest on was checked against source and all hold. The canonicaliser-overlap decision is correct on the evidence and is the right call. The REQ-199 extension is correctly scoped and does NOT push it past one agent turn. The webhook/signing.zig question is not a defect here. Zero blockers remain. Two observations are recorded as non-blocking notes for the implementing agents rather than as issues -- neither changes what gets built, and holding a 19-requirement batch at the escalation threshold over them would be exactly the 'mostly good' averaging this gate exists to avoid, in reverse.

fix_verification.defect: MAJOR (rework 1) -- src/repository exhaustiveness assertion false; four files unowned
fix_verification.verdict: FIXED at the root, not papered over
fix_verification.detail: The scoping judgement was verified against source, not asserted: artifacts.zig imports canonicaliser.zig (artifacts.zig L10 'const canonicaliser = @import("canonicaliser.zig")'), activation.zig imports artifacts.zig (activation.zig L10 'const artifacts_mod = @import("artifacts.zig")'), and schemas.zig imports neither (only std and pool). So the cohesion argument holds exactly as stated -- the first three are one subsystem split at R-Co's own REPO-01/02/03/04 versus REPO-08/09/10 seam, and schemas.zig is genuinely separable. Drafting two and deferring one is the right division, not a convenience. schemas.zig's deferral cites REQ-109's existing out-of-scope declaration plus the artifact_versions dependency, which is a real blocker: REQ-109 states form_schema_registry is OUT OF SCOPE and REPO-05 indexes artifact_versions, which REQ-202 only now creates.

exhaustiveness_independently_verified.verdict: CONFIRMED TRUE -- and I agree webhook/signing.zig is not a defect here
exhaustiveness_independently_verified.method: Ran my own file-by-file check rather than re-reading the doc's claim: enumerated every .zig file across all eight subsystems (the six second-batch ones plus the first batch's webhook/ and dlq/, including secrets/integration/), and tested each basename for a mention in docs/requirements.yaml or the stage doc. Result: exactly ONE file unnamed -- webhook/signing.zig. This independently reproduces ORCH's 41-file result.
exhaustiveness_independently_verified.webhook_signing_judgement: NOT A DEFECT IN THIS BATCH, agreed, on two independent grounds. (1) Scope: signing.zig is src/webhook/, which is the FIRST batch's territory (REQ-181-184) -- this batch's remit is the six remaining subsystems, so it is out of scope by construction and its absence from a second-batch coverage list is not an omission. (2) Substance: it is 43 lines exporting a single function, buildSignatureHeader, whose entire behaviour is the HMAC header format REQ-183's signing clause already specifies and whose AC already asserts ('deliver/3's signature is independently verifiable ... equals the value deliver/3 actually sent in the documented header'). It is a helper, not a subsystem -- there is no unbuilt behaviour hiding behind it. Requiring a separate requirement for it would be file-counting, not coverage.
exhaustiveness_independently_verified.doc_quality_note: The doc's exhaustiveness paragraph is now well-formed in a way worth preserving: it states the claim, names the verification method and date, enumerates the per-subsystem counts it was checked against, and records that rework 1 and rework 2 each found gaps precisely because the claim is falsifiable. That is a coverage contract, not a boast.

canonicaliser_overlap_decision.verdict: CORRECT -- the decision is right and the evidence for it is real
canonicaliser_overlap_decision.verification: Checked both sides against source. R-Co: canonicaliser.zig's header (L26-32) states 'Numbers are normalised: integers without decimal point; no exponent notation unless required', and serializeFloat (L119-129) implements exactly that -- an integer-valued float within the safe-integer range is printed with {d:.0}, dropping the decimal. Letflow: promotion_digest.ex's canonicalize/1 sorts map keys into a Jason.OrderedObject, maps over lists, stringifies non-boolean non-nil atoms, and then falls through to 'defp canonicalize(value), do: value' -- numbers hit that catch-all and pass through UNCHANGED. The two algorithms genuinely differ on number handling, so extending promotion_digest.ex would change its output for any plan containing an integer-valued float.
canonicaliser_overlap_decision.consequence_confirmed: The breakage is real and not hypothetical: plan_digest is PERSISTED (priv/repo/migrations/20260816200001_create_promotion_reviews.exs L57 'add :plan_digest, :string, null: false', with unique index uq_promotion_review_active_digest, and again in create_promotion_assertion_runs L63), and promotion_review_store.ex re-verifies a submitted digest against the STORED row (L128-129, PromotionDigest.verify_digest(row.plan_digest, plan_digest) -> :digest_mismatch). So changing canonicalisation would make every already-stored digest fail verification. Building a second canonicaliser is therefore the correct call, and REQ-202 does not merely assert this -- it pins it with an AC requiring a test that REQ-036's digest over a fixed fixture is UNCHANGED, plus an AC requiring promotion_digest.ex to be unmodified (git diff) and both moduledocs to cross-reference each other. That converts a rationale into an enforced invariant, which is the right treatment for a deliberate duplicate.
canonicaliser_overlap_decision.minor_label_correction: NON-BLOCKING, recorded for the implementer: REQ-202 attributes the breakage to 'REQ-036's INV-PRM-5'. INV-PRM-5 is actually the CONSTANT-TIME COMPARISON invariant (promotion_digest.ex L19; design/promotion_plan.md L602 'verify_digest/2 must not be ==/=:='), not a digest-stability invariant. The substantive claim -- that stored digests would stop verifying -- is correct and independently confirmed above; only the invariant label is imprecise. Not worth a rework cycle: the AC that enforces the behaviour is correctly written and does not depend on the label.

req_202_validation.a_testability: PASS -- 14 ACs, all falsifiable. Notably strong ones: dedup asserted by row counts across BOTH tables; canonical equivalence asserted across two differing serialisations of one document; number normalisation asserted on the canonical BYTES, not only the hash; binary artifacts asserted to equal a plain SHA-256 of submitted bytes; DB-level immutability asserted by a statement issued around the Ecto schema.
req_202_validation.b_consistency: PASS -- handles decision 0003 correctly, and better than a bare flag: it names the real tension (content-level dedup only spans tenants if the store is global, which makes one tenant's bytes physically shared with another's) and requires the placement to be decided, reasoned and REVIEWER-signed if global. It also pre-empts two collisions: REQ-036's promotion digest (see above) and REQ-041's solution_pack_artefact_bases, which it correctly identifies as an unrelated install-tracking table it neither reads nor writes.
req_202_validation.c_depends_on: PASS -- [REQ-036, REQ-072, REQ-067] is correct and minimal. REQ-036 is genuinely required: REQ-202 must not modify it and must assert its digests are unchanged, so it needs it built. REQ-067 for the version-history cursor, REQ-072 for tenancy. Nothing missing.
req_202_validation.d_stage_fit: PASS -- S6 cross-cutting; no route, correctly justified.
req_202_validation.e_size: PASS -- one subsystem (store + canonicaliser), split from activation at R-Co's own seam. Its description is the batch's longest (7490 chars) but that is evidence-density, not scope: the bulk is the migration-058 conflict record, the canonicaliser rationale and the two collision disambiguations, all of which constrain the implementer rather than adding deliverables.
req_202_validation.claims_verified: Migration 058 conflict CONFIRMED: 058_repo_artifacts_tenant_activation.sql L33-40 re-creates repository_artifacts with version_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, content_hash TEXT, content_json JSONB and parent_version_id -- a genuinely different shape from migration 045's, and both use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so the resulting shape really is order-dependent. This is a real upstream defect and REQ-202 is right to ship one shape and record which. REPO-11..14 'RELEASED but unwired' also CONFIRMED -- see below.

req_203_validation.a_testability: PASS -- 12 ACs. The REPO-08 criterion is correctly written as an OBSERVABILITY test (a concurrent read during an in-flight multi-artifact activation must see all-old or all-new, never a mix) rather than the weaker rollback check it could have settled for -- that distinction is drawn explicitly in the scope text and is the right reading of REPO-08.
req_203_validation.b_consistency: PASS -- and it resolves a genuine ambiguity rather than leaving it: it states that an activation produces BOTH a domain history row here AND a REQ-195 audit entry, explains why they are not duplicates (subsystem lineage with mandatory rationale versus tenant-wide hash-chained compliance trail), and requires the moduledoc to say so 'so a later reader does not delete one as redundant'. That is exactly the failure mode worth pre-empting.
req_203_validation.c_depends_on: PASS -- [REQ-202, REQ-072, REQ-067] correct and minimal; the FK to REQ-202's artifact_versions makes REQ-202 a hard prerequisite. Build order 202<203 holds.
req_203_validation.e_size: PASS -- three tables and the activation semantics, genuinely one turn, and correctly split from REQ-202 at R-Co's artifacts.zig/activation.zig boundary.

req_199_extension_sizing.verdict: CORRECTLY SCOPED -- has NOT grown past one agent turn
req_199_extension_sizing.reasoning: This was the question most likely to justify a FAIL, so I weighed it on substance rather than on the AC count alone. REQ-199 is now 18 ACs (from 15), the batch's largest. But the extension adds NO new schema, NO new table, NO new process and NO new mechanism: scope item 7 is two READ-ONLY figures computed directly off the two tables REQ-199 already creates -- per-correlation lag as max(sequence_no) minus applied_seq, and the age of the oldest PENDING row -- emitted through REQ-194's existing registry rather than a second counter mechanism. Verified against R-Co: observability.zig is 182 lines, its own header states it implements 'ORD-04 AC1/AC2: per-correlation lag (max(sequence_no) - applied_seq) and the age of the oldest PENDING row, read directly off plat_effect_completion joined...', and CorrelationLagRow carries exactly those two fields. So the requirement's definition matches upstream exactly and the work is a query plus two metric emissions. The three added ACs are correspondingly narrow (lag value on a stated fixture, oldest-pending age with a null-not-zero distinction, threshold event payload), and a fourth was AMENDED rather than added, to record that the measurement half is now in scope while the reduction half stays deferred. Splitting this into a separate requirement would be worse, not better: the figures are meaningless without the tables and cursor semantics in the same head, and a split would need its own depends_on back to REQ-199 for no gain. REQ-194 correctly added to depends_on since the registry is now consumed. The measurement/reduction split is honest -- it fixes exactly the gap that ORD-04 AC1/AC2 were being silently dropped while only AC3 was named as deferred.

repo_11_14_unwired_claim.verdict: CONFIRMED -- 'RELEASED but unwired' is accurate, and no route requirement is owed
repo_11_14_unwired_claim.evidence: Verified in R-Co directly, since this changes whether a route requirement is owed. grep for 'repository/artifacts', handleCreateArtifact and handleListVersions across R-Co's entire src/api/ returns ZERO matches -- no handler exists. authorization.zig has no repository or artifact policy key (grep returns nothing), so even the permission surface was never created. REPO-11 is indeed marked 'status: RELEASED' in R-Co's own docs/requirements.yaml with a release_decision pointing at docs/status/release-stage10-repo-20260528.json. So the requirement was released against a route that does not exist upstream. Letflow-side, I confirmed there is no SPA consumer either. Conclusion: there is genuinely nothing to port and no consumer contract to build to -- unlike REQ-191/192, REQ-194 and REQ-200, where a committed SPA client made the route obligatory. Recording it as not-covered item 5 with that reasoning is the correct treatment, and materially better than porting a phantom API on the strength of a RELEASED tag.

non_blocking_observations: REQ-202's 'INV-PRM-5' attribution is imprecise -- that invariant is constant-time comparison, not digest stability. The substantive claim (stored digests would stop verifying) is correct and separately confirmed via the persisted plan_digest column and promotion_review_store.ex's verify_digest gate. The enforcing AC is correctly written and label-independent, so this is a note for the implementing agent, not a rework item.

REQ-202 and REQ-203 both defer their placement decision (per-tenant versus global) to the implementing requirement with a REVIEWER sign-off requirement, matching REQ-189/191/201's established treatment. Consistent across the batch; no drift.

REQ-199 at 18 ACs is now the batch's largest and should be watched at WF-02 time -- not because its scope is wrong, but because if its implementer finds the lag surface expanding beyond two read-only figures, that is the signal to split scope item 7 into its own requirement rather than to grow this one further.

The batch's three-iteration arc is worth recording: each rework found a genuine defect the previous one had not, and each was found because the previous iteration made a vaguer statement falsifiable. The stage doc's coverage claim moved from an implied range, to an asserted exhaustiveness, to a machine-verified per-file mapping. That progression is the reason the src/repository gap surfaced at all.
All findings from the original iteration and rework 1 remain resolved; no regression introduced. REQ-199 is the only previously-committed batch entry modified, and its modification is additive.
